paper_design_summary: Two online Prolific experiments compare human work under different LLM assistance arrangements; the method of assigning people to the main assistance conditions is not stated. Experiment 1 analyzed 315 people on unassisted SAT-level math after lessons with no agents, a tutor, two peers, or tutor plus peers, and is outside the creativity scope (pp. 3-5, Sections 3.1-3.2). Experiment 2 analyzed 247 people who each wrote a creative and an argumentative essay with Control, Single, or Duo support; GPT-5.2 scored essay quality and SBERT similarity of extracted key points measured diversity across writers while assistance was available in the AI arms (pp. 5-8, Sections 4.1-4.2).

studies.label: Experiment 1: Math problem solving with LLM tutor and peers (outside creativity scope)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants worked under Control, Tutor Only, Peers Only, or Tutor + Peers. The method of allocating people to these assistance conditions is not stated. Figure 1 specifies random topic selection; peer speaking order is also randomized. Neither establishes random allocation to AI assistance (pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and sections 3.1.2-3.1.4).
assignment.quote: participants were introduced to the task and to the agents assigned to their condition (where applicable).

arms.name: Control
arms.description: No chat interface or agent feedback during the lesson (p. 3, section 3.1.2).

arms.name: Tutor Only
arms.description: Bob, a GPT-5.2 tutor, gives feedback and follow-up questions (pp. 2-3, sections 3.1.1-3.1.2).

arms.name: Peers Only
arms.description: Two GPT-5.2 peers: Alice makes arithmetic errors, and Charlie makes conceptual errors; peers discuss alternative solutions with the participant (p. 3, sections 3.1.1-3.1.2).

arms.name: Tutor + Peers
arms.description: The GPT-5.2 tutor and both GPT-5.2 peers interact with the participant; the tutor gives feedback and selects respondents (p. 3, section 3.1.2).

participants.exclusions: 614 people were recruited; 315 passed preregistered attention and authenticity checks and constitute the analyzed sample. The paper does not give the recruitment count as a randomized count, report exact per-arm counts, or state how many exclusions occurred after condition allocation (p. 4, section 3.1.5).
participants.who: Prolific workers, fluent in English, with at least a 99% approval rating and at least 100 completed tasks (p. 4, section 3.1.5).
participants.quote: Following our preregistered exclusion criteria, only 315 participants passed our attention and authenticity checks

ai_tool.how_used: Role-prompted tutor and/or error-prone peer agents in free-form text chat during lessons; participants could ask questions at any time. All agents were removed for the subsequent test (pp. 2-4, sections 3.1.1-3.1.4).

task.description: SAT-level mathematics: probability, linear equations, average speed, group means, and systems of equations. Participants attempted lesson problems in two categories and later solved isomorphic variants without assistance. This is mathematical learning/retention, not a convergent creativity test (p. 4, sections 3.1.3-3.1.4).
task.duration: A 5-minute lesson per problem in agent conditions, followed by a 1-minute Tetris distractor before the unassisted test; approximately 14 minutes overall (p. 4, sections 3.1.4-3.1.5).

studies.label: Experiment 2: Co-writing creative and argumentative essays with LLM collaborators

assignment.what_was_assigned: The main assistance conditions are Control, Single, and Duo in a between-subjects design. Assignment of people among these conditions is not explicitly described as random. Essay prompts, essay order, the GPT-5.2 versus Claude Opus 4.6 identity within Single, and model-to-role mapping within Duo are explicitly randomized. No output contrasts by the randomized model identity or role mapping are reported (pp. 5-6, sections 4-4.1.3; p. 8, sections 4.2.1-4.2.2).
assignment.locator: p. 5, section 4 and sections 4.1.1-4.1.2; p. 6, section 4.1.3
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 5, footnote 2: https://aspredicted.org/gq922f.pdf; p. 8, section 4.1.5 explicitly refers to pre-registered exclusion criteria. The linked registration could not be retrieved because network access was blocked.

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Participants write essays without AI assistance (p. 5, section 4).

arms.name: Single
arms.description: One generalist writing assistant, randomly GPT-5.2 or Claude Opus 4.6, supplies concise feedback of no more than 50 words per message; free-form chat is available while writing (pp. 5-6, sections 4.1.2-4.1.3).

arms.name: Duo
arms.description: GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6 are both available with complementary roles: imagination/voice versus craft/structure for creative writing, and dialectical critique versus logic/evidence for argumentative writing. Model-to-role assignment is randomized; agents build on each other's feedback (pp. 5-6, section 4.1.2).

participants.exclusions: 419 people were recruited; 247 people were analyzed after preregistered exclusions based on an attention check and a minimum of 40 words in both essays. Each analyzed participant produced two usable essays. The paper reports an approximately 41% attrition rate. Counts at random assignment, per-arm analyzed counts, and the timing of exclusions relative to condition allocation are not given (p. 8, Section 4.1.5).
participants.who: English-fluent Prolific workers with at least a 99% approval rating and at least 100 completed tasks (p. 8, section 4.1.5).
participants.quote: 247 of the 419 recruited participants produced two usable essays

ai_tool.how_used: The Single generalist and Duo specialists comment on the participant's developing essay. Agents can see the current essay text, and Single feedback is limited to 50 words per message; Duo agents acknowledge and build on each other's feedback. Participants can also initiate questions and discussions through free-form text chat throughout writing. Refinement is the primary role code because the specified assistance is feedback on the person's own draft; open chat describes an additional interaction mode (p. 5, Section 4.1.2; p. 6, Sections 4.1.2-4.1.3).

task.description: Each participant wrote an argumentative essay and a creative essay, approximately 200-300 words each, with one prompt randomly selected from a pool of 3 per essay type and randomized essay order. Prompts were drawn from the New York Times Student Opinion series. Assigned assistance remained available during production of the scored essays; there is no later unassisted writing assessment (pp. 5-6, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3; p. 10, Section 5.2).
task.duration: Section 4.1.1 says at least 5 minutes per essay (p. 5), whereas Section 4.1.3 says a 5-minute time limit (p. 6). Median total completion time was 11 minutes (p. 8, Section 4.1.5).

outcomes.name: Combined essay quality (creative and argumentative essays)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-5.2 rates each essay dimension on a 1-5 scale. The creative rubric includes originality, narrative structure and coherence, elaboration and richness, expressiveness and emotional impact, and literary quality and language use; the argumentative rubric includes argument clarity, strength of evidence and reasoning, logical structure and organization, integration of counterarguments, persuasiveness, and language and formality (p. 6, section 4.1.4). The analyzed combined outcome averages each participant's creative and argumentative essay scores and is reported on a 1-5 scale (p. 7, Figure 7a; p. 8, section 4.2.1). Section 4.1.4 instead describes summing dimension ratings to produce each essay composite; the normalization needed to reconcile these descriptions is not stated. Two independent human raters validated a subset of 83 essays (49 creative, 34 argumentative): human inter-rater Pearson r = .87; human-GPT composite agreement Spearman rho = .77 for creative and .73 for argumentative essays (p. 7, section 4.1.4). These validation essays and raters are not the participant analysis count. OLS predicting combined quality from condition: F(2, 244) = 21.91, p < .0001, R² = 0.152; planned pairwise comparisons use Bonferroni correction (p. 8, section 4.2.1). Figure 7a shows means and ±1 SEM without numerical arm means or error-bar values (p. 7).

contrasts.reported: Control vs. Single: Δ = 0.332, t(244) = 6.21, p < .0001; Single has higher combined essay quality. Bonferroni-corrected planned comparison; numerical arm SDs and SEs are not reported.
Control vs. Duo: Δ = 0.234, t(244) = 4.21, p = 0.0001; Duo has higher combined essay quality. Bonferroni-corrected planned comparison; numerical arm SDs and SEs are not reported.

As printed, Single vs. Duo: Δ = 0.098, t(244) = 1.56, p = 0.363. Single has the higher mean, but the difference is not significant. The printed comparison is retained in its original orientation; this record names Duo as treatment and Single as control. Bonferroni-corrected planned comparison.

outcomes.name: Idea-level diversity across writers (key-point cosine similarity)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: gpt-5-mini extracts 3-5 atomic key points per essay: claims for argumentative essays and narrative elements or themes for creative essays. A sentence transformer (SBERT; exact checkpoint not stated) embeds these points. Mean pairwise cosine similarity is computed within condition-by-prompt cells and aggregated across prompts (p. 7, section 4.1.4). Similarity is inversely oriented to diversity. Methods explicitly call this the secondary outcome, although the Figure 7 caption calls both displayed outcomes primary (p. 7). No separate results by essay type or prompt are reported.

contrasts.reported: Mean similarity: Single: 0.748 vs. Control: 0.735; permutation p = .033. Higher similarity means lower diversity, so the direction is coded as treatment_lower for diversity.
Mean similarity: Duo: 0.737 vs. Control: 0.735; p = .950 (permutation procedure described in section 4.1.4).
Mean similarity: Duo: 0.737; Single: 0.748; Duo vs. Single: p = .065. The paper describes Duo as marginally less homogenized than Single; the difference does not reach .05.

diversity_detail.metric: Mean pairwise cosine similarity of LLM-extracted atomic key-point embeddings; higher similarity means less diversity (p. 7, section 4.1.4).
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence transformer (SBERT); exact model/checkpoint not stated (p. 7, section 4.1.4).
diversity_detail.computed_over: All key points within each condition-by-prompt cell, using bootstrap samples of essays; cell similarities are aggregated across prompts to obtain a condition-level score (p. 7, section 4.1.4). The text does not specify whether pairs of key points from the same essay are excluded.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: For each cell, sample n = 15 essays with replacement and repeat for M = 1,000 rounds, yielding a mean and 95% confidence interval per cell. For each condition pair, pool essays, shuffle condition labels, recompute the difference in mean bootstrapped similarity, and repeat for M = 1,000 rounds; p is the proportion of absolute permuted differences at least as large as observed (p. 7, section 4.1.4). Figure 7b specifies error bars of ±1 SEM; numerical intervals or SEs are not printed. The method describes essay resampling and does not state whether the two essays from a participant remain grouped.
diversity_detail.notes: The unit is the condition/prompt set underlying the aggregate comparison, rather than an independently analyzed person or key-point pair. Total numbers of key points and pairs are not stated. The bootstrap n = 15 is a number of sampled essays, not the number of participants analyzed. Diversity directions reverse the interpretation of similarity; printed means and p-values are preserved without computing an effect size. The methods call diversity secondary, whereas Figure 7 labels the displayed outcomes primary; the primary field follows the explicit outcome hierarchy in Section 4.1.4. The methods' bootstrap confidence intervals and the figure's SEM caption are both retained without equating them.

sample_overlap.locator: No participant-sharing or reanalysis statement was found in the complete document. Recruitment is described in p. 4, Section 3.1.5 and p. 8, Section 4.1.5. Reuse of math problem templates or writing prompts is not evidence of participant overlap.

company_involvement.description: No company affiliation, funding, or other company involvement is stated. All author affiliations are University of Toronto; the acknowledgments thank individuals for graphics and discussion.

eligibility.reason: Experiment 2 meets criterion 2 with 247 analyzed people, each contributing two usable essays after exclusions (p. 8, Section 4.1.5). Criterion 3 is met by GPT-5.2 ratings of participant-produced essays, including originality, and computed similarity of essay key points across writers (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1.4; p. 8, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2). Single and Duo assistance was available during writing (p. 6, Section 4.1.3). Criterion 1 remains unclear: Control, Single, and Duo constitute a between-subjects design, but allocation among these main assistance conditions is not stated to be random. Explicit randomization concerns prompts, essay order, model identity within Single, and model-to-role mapping within Duo; no reported output contrast isolates either randomized AI configuration (pp. 5-6, Sections 4-4.1.3; p. 8, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2). Both linked preregistration PDFs were requested during finalization and failed with WinError 10013, so they cannot settle allocation. Both design_class values remain other because neither randomized nor nonrandom main-arm allocation is established. Experiment 1 analyzed 315 people but measures ordinary SAT-level mathematical learning, outside the creativity scope, and cannot establish this paper's core eligibility (p. 4, Sections 3.1.3-3.1.5; p. 10, Section 5.2).

one_line_finding: Among 247 analyzed writers, Single and Duo had higher combined essay quality than Control (reported differences 0.332 and 0.234), Single had higher idea similarity (0.748 vs. 0.735; p = .033), and Duo did not clearly differ in similarity from Control (0.737 vs. 0.735; p = .950) or Single (p = .065; p. 8, Sections 4.1.5 and 4.2.1-4.2.2).
open_questions: Was assignment to the main assistance conditions randomized in either experiment? The PDF does not state the allocation method, and both linked AsPredicted PDFs failed with WinError 10013 during reconciliation (pp. 2-6, Sections 3-4.1.3).
What were the assigned and analyzed counts in each arm, and which exclusions occurred after assignment? Only recruitment and retained totals are printed (p. 4, Section 3.1.5; p. 8, Section 4.1.5).
Where is the Appendix with the math-agent system prompts? It is referenced on p. 2, Section 3.1.1 but absent from the saved PDF, which ends on p. 12.

How were the summed rubric dimensions converted to the reported 1-5 combined quality score, and are component-specific results or numerical arm means, SDs, and SEs available (pp. 6-8, Section 4.1.4, Figure 7a, and Section 4.2.1)?
Which SBERT checkpoint was used, were same-essay key-point pairs excluded, and did essay resampling preserve participant grouping across the two essays (p. 7, Section 4.1.4)?

How do the bootstrap 95% confidence intervals described in the methods relate to the error bars labeled as SEM in Figure 7? Neither numeric bounds nor a reconciliation is printed (p. 7, Section 4.1.4 and Figure 7).
Was the writing duration a minimum or a maximum of 5 minutes per essay? Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.3 use different descriptions (pp. 5-6).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from two present, parseable raw forms. The entire 64,398-character markdown conversion was read in consecutive chunks through the references; no appendix is included. Relevant PDF pages were independently extracted with PyMuPDF, and Figures 1 and 7 were inspected directly in memory. Every retained numerical claim was checked against the PDF; no effect size, standard error, per-arm participant count, or unstated output count was computed. The outcome inventory retains the combined essay-quality measure, cross-writer idea similarity, and all eleven explicitly scored rubric dimensions. The component outcomes have empty contrasts because no dimension-specific condition results are reported. Human ratings of 83 essays validate the automated measure and do not supply a separate treatment outcome or participant count. Self-reported confidence, helpfulness, idea stimulation, confusion, and agent perceptions are excluded because they do not score creative outputs. Math test performance is outside the creativity scope. The abstract's 562 is the paper-wide total, not the writing study's sample (p. 1; analyzed study counts on pp. 4 and 8). Refinement is selected for the writing assistants because their specified role is feedback on a developing draft; participant-initiated chat is retained in how_used. Counterargument integration maps to usefulness as a rubric component assessing writing quality. There are three substantive field-level differences: AI-role coding, the counterargument construct, and inclusion of the Duo-Control result in the one-line finding. Differences of wording, added locators, movement of the same statistics between fields, and empty synthesis defaults are not counted. Both forms give the same outcome inventory, design codes, assignment status/unit/structure, participant counts, arms, outcome questions, measures, units, availability, timing, primary codes, reported numerical statistics, supplement status, absence of stated sample sharing or company involvement, and eligibility codes. The Figure 7 primary/secondary inconsistency noted by B is retained; both forms already code diversity secondary. n_unresolved counts unresolved screener differences only; agreed source uncertainties remain in open_questions, with random assistance allocation marked unconfirmed in agreed_fields_checked. Both named AsPredicted URLs were retried with Python urllib and User-Agent atlas-screening/0.1, without personal identifiers, and both failed with WinError 10013. No external material was retrieved. challenge_resolution.problem: S1 assignment.randomized: the challenge disputes a categorical randomized-experiment claim while acknowledging that the form already records not_stated.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: No correction to the form: retained randomized = not_stated, design_class = other, and null randomized counts. The checker correctly identifies missing evidence, but the stronger claim it disputes is absent from the reconciled form. The source mentions agents assigned to a condition without specifying random allocation among the four assistance arms; random topic/question selection, peer responding order, and approximate balance do not supply that procedure. The underlying allocation question remains open, but S1 is outside the creativity scope and does not affect paper eligibility.

challenge_resolution.problem: S2 assignment.randomized: the challenge disputes random allocation among Control, Single, and Duo while acknowledging that the form already records not_stated and criterion 1 as unclear.
challenge_resolution.what_changed: No correction to the existing coding: retained randomized = not_stated, design_class = other, and unclear for criterion 1 and core eligibility. The checker agrees with these values; its refutation concerns a stronger randomized-experiment claim absent from the form. The source states a between-subjects design and explicitly randomizes prompts, task order, model identity within Single, and model-to-role mapping within Duo. The reported output contrasts pool those model configurations within the three main arms, so those within-arm randomizations do not verify allocation for the coded contrasts. Neither random nor nonrandom main-arm allocation is established. The underlying S2 question is retained as an eligibility open item; both linked preregistrations were inaccessible during finalization.

open_items.item: open_questions[0], S2: Was allocation to Control, Single, and Duo randomized? This affects criterion 1. Author confirmation of the implemented allocation procedure would settle it; the linked writing preregistration at https://aspredicted.org/gq922f.pdf could provide supporting documentation but was inaccessible (pp. 5-6, Sections 4-4.1.3).

open_questions[0], S1: Was allocation to Control, Tutor Only, Peers Only, and Tutor + Peers randomized? Author confirmation of the implemented allocation procedure would settle the design question. It does not affect this paper's creativity eligibility because S1 has no qualifying creativity or diversity outcome (pp. 3-4, Figure 1 and Sections 3.1.2-3.1.5). The linked math preregistration at https://aspredicted.org/rq8uz9.pdf was inaccessible.

open_questions[1]: Exact assigned and analyzed counts by arm and exclusions before versus after assignment are unreported. Participant-level allocation and exclusion records would settle these counts. They affect extraction and attrition assessment, not criterion 2: S2 independently establishes 247 analyzed people across its arms (p. 4, Section 3.1.5; p. 8, Section 4.1.5).

open_questions[2]: The Appendix containing math-agent system prompts is referenced but absent from the saved PDF. Obtaining that supplement would settle the missing prompt documentation; it affects no eligibility criterion for the writing study (p. 2, Section 3.1.1; pp. 10-12, References through the end).

open_questions[3]: The conversion from summed rubric dimensions to the reported 1-5 combined quality score, dimension-specific results, and numerical arm means, SDs, and SEs remain unspecified. Essay scores and analysis code would settle the aggregation and statistical extraction questions. They do not change criterion 3 because originality and diversity are explicitly scored on produced essays (pp. 6-8, Section 4.1.4, Figure 7a, and Section 4.2.1).

open_questions[4]: The exact SBERT checkpoint, treatment of same-essay key-point pairs, and participant grouping during resampling are unstated. Analysis code and essay-to-participant identifiers would settle these reproducibility and uncertainty questions. They affect extraction and precision assessment, not whether diversity was computed on participant outputs (p. 7, Section 4.1.4).

open_questions[5]: The relationship between the methods' 95% bootstrap confidence intervals and Figure 7's SEM error bars remains unexplained. Author clarification identifying each uncertainty measure and its numerical values would settle the discrepancy. It affects uncertainty extraction, not any eligibility criterion (p. 7, Section 4.1.4 and Figure 7).

open_questions[6]: Whether the five-minute writing duration was a minimum or a maximum remains inconsistent between Sections 4.1.1 and 4.1.3. Author confirmation of the implemented timing rule would settle it. It affects the task description, not any eligibility criterion (pp. 5-6; p. 10, Section 5.2 also describes time-bounded five-minute writing sessions).
